edges.description: The tumour-associated lymphoid response is the mechanism this entry attributes childhood opsoclonus to, but how it reaches the brainstem and cerebellar circuits that generate opsoclonus is not established: no antigen is identified, and whether the effector arm is humoral or T-cell mediated is open.
Myoclonus is the second component of the same syndrome and is attributed to the same tumour-associated response; the intermediate steps are no better established than for opsoclonus.

nodes.description: A third mechanism arm, and the one that fits neither of this entry's two antibody-defined subtypes. In children, opsoclonus-myoclonus syndrome is the paraneoplastic syndrome characteristic of neuroblastic tumours: about half of children presenting with OMS in referral cohorts are found to have a tumour, and in those the tumour is neuroblastic, most often neuroblastoma. The tumours of affected children carry a distinctive immune infiltrate - diffuse and extensive lymphocytic infiltration with lymphoid follicles, which matched controls do not show - and that infiltrate is a polyclonal expansion of both B and T cells organised into tertiary lymphoid structures, with no single antigenic stimulus identified. Commercially screened serum autoantibodies are negative in this setting while cerebrospinal fluid oligoclonal bands and B cells are present, so the humoral signal is intrathecal rather than a serum antibody. Which arm of the response injures the brain is unsettled; see the knowledge gap in discussions.

evidence.reference_title: Opsoclonus-myoclonus-ataxia syndrome in neuroblastoma: histopathologic features-a report from the Children's Cancer Group.
evidence.snippet: Pathology slides from a total of 54 neuroblastoma tumors were reviewed blindly. They included 13 tumors associated with opsoclonus-myoclonus and 41 age- and stage-matched controls. ... Twelve of 13 cases had diffuse (found in every section prepared from the multiple portions of the primary tumor) and extensive (occupying more than 50% of a single of multiple microscopic fields with x 100 magnification) lymphocytic infiltration with lymphoid follicles. Of the 41 control cases (27 FH and 14 UH tumors), 18 had focal areas of lymphocytic infiltration and six showed lymphoid follicles, but none had diffuse or extensive infiltration in their primary tumors.
